extracted.intended_audience: patent drafters, patent attorneys/agents preparing claim language for international filings (PCT, EPO, USPTO)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for drafting claim language and claim sets in patent applications, covering claim structure, terminology, dependent/independent claims, functional/Markush/means-plus-function formulations, and jurisdictional drafting practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim structure and punctuation
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim should have a preamble, a transitional phrase, and a body made of elements typically separated by semicolons, with the penultimate element followed by "; and," and the last element ending with a full stop. In some countries each element or combination of elements is separated by line indentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model: Preamble, transitional phrase: – – – Element (#1); Element (#2); and Element (#3). Example: 'An apparatus, comprising: a plurality of printed pages; a binding configured to hold the printed pages together; and a cover attached to the binding.' Follow local practice on indentation (e.g., US often requires indentation; other countries accept but do not require it).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper antecedent basis
rubrics_metrics.description: Each element must introduce terms with an indefinite article ('a' or 'an') on first use and refer back with a definite article ('the') thereafter; antecedent basis must be re-established for each new claim set.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example claim set shows 'a pencil' introduced in Claim 1, later referred to as 'the pencil' in dependent claims. If introducing multiple similar items, distinguish them (e.g., 'first' and 'second' or 'an' and 'another'). Each new claim set must independently establish antecedent basis. Note: 'said' and 'the' are interchangeable but 'said' is older legalese—many jurisdictions prefer plain language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference numerals and parenthetical expressions
rubrics_metrics.description: In some jurisdictions (including PCT practice) reference numerals that label drawings may be recited in parentheses after corresponding elements in the claims to aid comprehension; such numerals are generally not to be interpreted as limiting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'a plurality of printed pages (11)'. Be cautious: (i) in some countries (notably US) including reference numerals is avoided or prohibited because they may be interpreted as limiting; (ii) adding text inside parentheses (e.g., 'securing means (screw 13, nail 14)') can create 'special features' and unintended limits; (iii) parenthetical notes without numerals (e.g., '(concrete) molded brick') can cause clarity objections. If used, consider adding a statement in the description that numerals are non-limiting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special claim words and transitional phrases
rubrics_metrics.description: Words and phrases such as 'comprising', 'wherein', 'whereby', 'such that', 'so as to', and 'configured to' carry particular meanings in claims and must be used with an understanding of their legal interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 'Comprising' is open-ended (typically), 'wherein' often introduces a function/operation/result that flows from previously recited structure and should be used where the result necessarily follows. The drafter must know how courts in target jurisdictions interpret these words and choose phrasing appropriate to the protection sought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement for multiple elements (avoid single-element overbreadth)
rubrics_metrics.description: Many patent offices require claims to recite at least two elements; a single-element claim may be impossibly broad and read on unrelated items.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare a claim 'A computer, comprising: a processor.' (too broad) with a claim that recites processor, memory, and bus (appropriately structured). Ensure the claim provides sufficient structure/limitations to avoid being unacceptably broad.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-part (Jepson/improvement) claims
rubrics_metrics.description: A two-part claim sets out the most relevant known prior art in the preamble and characterizes the improvement in the body, connected by a transitional phrase (e.g., 'characterized by', 'characterized in that', or 'wherein the improvement comprises').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pros: clearly highlights the inventive contribution over the prior art and is preferred in some offices (e.g., EPO). Cons: it constitutes an admission that the preamble part was known, which may be undesirable. Use when invention is a distinct improvement on an old combination; avoid when it would give a misleading picture (e.g., combination of known integers of equal status, modifications of a known chemical process, complex interrelated systems, or new chemical compounds). Consider drafting standard-format claims first and adopting two-part format if required by examiner or advantageous for filings limited to jurisdictions that prefer it.

rubrics_metrics.name: EPO guidance for two-part claims
rubrics_metrics.description: For two-part claims the EPO recommends the first part state the designation of the subject matter (general technical class) and technical features necessary for defining the claimed subject matter which are part of the prior art; the characterizing part should summarize the added features.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply this formatting where appropriate (e.g., where the invention is an improvement on an old combination). Be mindful that the first part applies only to independent claims and that the EPO preference is flexible—claims not in two-part form are common in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternative elements and Markush groups
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims may include alternative elements, but ordinary 'or' expressions can lack clarity. Markush claim style ('selected from the group consisting of X, Y and Z') is commonly used (especially in chemical claims) to claim alternatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an inclusive 'or' is meant, use 'and/or', 'at least one selected from', or equivalent language. If multiple members can be selected simultaneously, explicitly state 'and combinations thereof'. Markush groups must not be ambiguous and should be used cautiously: if one alternative is anticipated in the prior art, the whole Markush claim can lack novelty. Consider claiming members in separate dependent claims where appropriate. Markush useful in chemical claims; in other fields prefer a generic term where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional elements and means-plus-function claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Functional language (defining elements by what they do rather than structure) may be used provided a person skilled in the art can perform the function without inventive skill; means-plus-function claims recite 'means for [function]' and are interpreted variably across jurisdictions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Means-plus-function claims can be helpful where they are interpreted more broadly, but can also be interpreted narrowly (limited to structures disclosed in the specification and their equivalents). Not all claim elements need be means elements; mix types if useful. Expect jurisdiction-specific differences and changing case law over a patent's lifetime—draft with these uncertainties in mind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification support for functional/means claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Means-plus-function claims typically require adequate description in the specification of specific structures that perform the recited functions; otherwise the claims risk narrow construction or rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide clear disclosure of the structures (e.g., list example structures like 'tapes, adhesives, rivets') that perform the function. Avoid failing to identify which structures perform which functions and avoid reciting unnecessary structures that could invite narrow interpretation. If all elements are purely functional without structure, risk rejection as a mere desideratum (a desired result without how it is achieved).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim sets strategy (independent and dependent claims)
rubrics_metrics.description: A typical claim set contains one or more independent claims and multiple dependent claims; at least one independent claim must define the essential features needed to meet patentability requirements (novelty, inventive step).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft a broad independent claim to capture the broadest protection and multiple dependent claims of narrower scope as fallbacks. Balance the number and breadth of claims against filing/examination/maintenance fees and administrative limits (some offices charge per-claim fees or limit independent claims per category). Vary claim breadth to provide insurance against later-found prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number and breadth of claims—costs and administrative limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent laws rarely set an upper claim limit, but many offices impose fees for excess claims or limit independent claims per category (e.g., EPO), so drafters must weigh costs against protection gained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider office-specific counting rules (some count only numbered claims; USPTO charges for multiple dependent claims even if not separately numbered). Over-proliferation of claims increases fees and complexity; choose a reasonable number proportional to the invention's complexity and client's budget.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independent claim content: essential features and clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Independent claims should specify the essential features that define the invention and any features necessary for the technical effect; claims must be clear and directed to the heart of the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the invention's patentability rests on a technical effect, include the features essential to achieve it. For product claims of a known kind modified in specified ways, clearly identify the known product and the modifications. For process claims, ensure the process reasonably leads to the claimed product to avoid internal inconsistency and clarity problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dependent claim form, scope and drafting effect
rubrics_metrics.description: A dependent claim 'depends from' another claim, includes all features of the parent claim even if not explicitly repeated, and narrows the scope relative to its parent; dependent claims are shorter and serve to define specific embodiments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Format dependencies by referencing the parent claim (e.g., 'The apparatus of Claim 1, further comprising: ...'). Be aware that dependent claims are narrower than the independent claim. Use dependent claims to claim preferred embodiments and to provide fallbacks if broad claims are attacked by prior art. Examples in the manual show how dependent claims incorporate parent text and further limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dependent claims as fallback protection
rubrics_metrics.description: Dependent claims serve as fallback positions: if a broad independent claim is rejected (e.g., by prior art), narrower dependent claims may still be allowable and provide practical protection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft dependent claims covering narrower ranges, particular configurations, or preferred features that might survive if the broad claim is invalidated. Use dependent claims strategically to preserve commercially important claim scope while managing prosecution risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity and conciseness requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims must be clear and concise as a matter of law; excessive, ambiguous, or convoluted claim drafting can lead to objections or rejections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid unclear parenthetical expressions, ambiguous alternatives, or overly lengthy two-part claims where inappropriate. Keep the number of dependent claims reasonable to avoid undue complication. Draft as if claims must be understandable without reference to drawings (claims are not to incorporate drawings).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid claiming mere desideratum
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that define all elements only functionally without disclosure of how to achieve them risk being rejected as claiming a mere desideratum (a desired result without specifying how it is achieved).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the specification provides sufficient detail and structure for any functional limitations. If all claim elements are functional, include supporting structural disclosure to avoid objections for lack of clarity or sufficiency.
